regelverk.gapLead: The measurement is one source. HSE describes surveys as one technique among several for assessing the current situation, and the risk assessment must be acted on. This lies outside Orgpuls today:

gap.policy: A written health and safety policy, with the organisation and arrangements for carrying it out, brought to every employee’s notice — from five employees (HSWA 1974 s.2(3), SI 1975/1584)

gap.procedures: Agreed policies and procedures to prevent or resolve unacceptable behaviour, and a way to report it (Management Standards: Relationships)
gap.environment: The physical work environment, and whether skills and jobs match the demands (Management Standards: Demands) — not measured
gap.competent: Competent assistance with your health and safety duties, in-house where you employ someone suitable (MHSWR 1999 reg 7)
gap.consultation: Consulting employees or their representatives before the survey, which the duty to consult in good time supports (SRSC 1977 reg 4A, HSCER 1996 reg 3) — Orgpuls records it, but the consultation is yours

hswa2.what: The general duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all employees (in Northern Ireland, art. 4 of the 1978 Order). Orgpuls serves it for work-related stress.

mhswr3.what: A suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks to employees, stress included, reviewed when it may no longer be valid; from five employees, a record of its significant findings and of any group especially at risk. Orgpuls documents the steps.

mhswr5.what: Arrangements for the effective planning, organisation, control, monitoring and review of the measures, recorded from five employees. Orgpuls holds the action plan and its follow-up; the arrangements are the employer’s to record.

hseStandards.what: HSE’s guidance on work-related stress, not law: six areas — Demands, Control, Support, Relationships, Role and Change. Following the approach correctly is one way to make the risk assessment suitable and sufficient.

consultation.what: Consult union-appointed safety representatives, elected representatives of employee safety, or employees directly, in good time on health and safety matters. There is no headcount rule, and the employer does not choose the representative.

ukgdpr.what: The survey processes personal data: legal obligation, not consent; employees may complain to the employer as controller (DPA 2018 s.164A); the regulator is the Information Commission (ICO). Results are shown only for groups that reach the threshold.

selskap.leadManual: You enter the name and company number yourselves. The industry you are compared against is chosen below.

body.p2: Then check groups and the threshold. The groups decide what you can break the results down by, and should follow where people actually work together. The threshold decides how many answers a group needs before it is shown on its own. Five is the default, and the lowest you can choose in the UK.
body.p3: Finally, set the measurement up under Measurement setup. That is where you record that the health and safety representative was consulted, or the employees directly where you have none (HSCER 1996 reg 4) — not a checkbox, but the record of their involvement. Only then can the round be planned.

velgTerskel.lead: Why five is the lowest in the UK, what happens to groups below the threshold, and when a higher one may be right.

body.p2: Five is the default and the lowest an organisation in the UK can choose: the floor is enforced by the database, which always counts with at least five, whatever the settings say. You can raise it to at most ten if you want to be stricter. A change applies to surveys not yet opened; a survey already open keeps the threshold employees answered under.
body.p3: The reason is not health and safety law but data protection law. In a small group a result can in practice be traced back to individuals, and then it is no longer anonymous figures — it is personal data. The Information Commission (ICO) points out that a person can be identifiable even if you do not know their name.
body.p4: The consequence is worth planning for: if you have many small departments, you get few figures to steer by. It is then usually better to merge groups that actually work together.

body.p3: The notification order is not optional. Safety and union representatives are notified first, then the managing director, then the line managers, and last everybody. The reason is that representatives should be consulted in good time, before the survey starts (SRSC 1977 reg 4A, HSCER 1996 reg 3), and a wheel that notified everybody at once would skip that. How far in advance the notices go is yours to change.

Use them for what the instrument does not cover and that is specific to you — a reorganisation, a new rota, a move. Avoid questions about health: the ICO counts a questionnaire that detects health problems as health information, which is special category data, and a well-meant “how are you really doing?” is closer to that line than it looks.

body.p1: Share the findings within two weeks. It is the single thing that decides the response rate next time, and it is also what the law assumes: employees must be given comprehensible and relevant information on the risks found and on the measures (MHSWR 1999 reg 10). A survey that is not shared is not a system, it is a questionnaire.
body.p4: The effect is measured by the next pulse, which asks about exactly the factors that have open measures. That is the chain of MHSWR 1999 regs 3 and 5: assess the risk, act on it, then monitor and review the measures.

body.p1: The legal basis is legal obligation, UK GDPR article 6(1)(c), the obligation being the risk assessment under MHSWR 1999 reg 3 and HSWA 1974 s.2. Not consent.
body.p3: The questions are written not to collect health data, which is special category data under UK GDPR article 9. The screening for offensive behaviour and violence is reported as counts only.
body.p2: That is not a technicality. Consent must be freely given, and an employee cannot consent freely to their employer — the power relationship is uneven. The survey also serves the risk assessment the employer must make in any case (MHSWR 1999 reg 3), and a consent that cannot be withdrawn without that duty falling away is not a consent.

hvaLovenKrever.title: What health and safety law actually requires
hvaLovenKrever.lead: HSWA 1974 s.2, MHSWR 1999 regs 3 and 5, and HSE’s Management Standards. What Orgpuls covers, and what you need elsewhere.

body.p1: Every employer must make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks to employees’ health and safety, stress included (MHSWR 1999 reg 3), and act on it under the general duty to ensure their health, safety and welfare so far as is reasonably practicable (HSWA 1974 s.2). From five employees the significant findings and any group especially at risk must be recorded (reg 3(6)), and so must the arrangements for planning, organisation, control, monitoring and review of the measures (reg 5). Orgpuls covers these steps for work-related stress and documents them.
body.p2: No statute or regulation names psychosocial factors. HSE’s Management Standards, which are guidance and not law, describe six areas: Demands, Control, Support, Relationships, Role and Change. HSE considers the approach suitable and sufficient if it is followed correctly, and does not expect every standard to be met. The instrument is mapped onto five of the areas; Change is touched by one statement only.
body.p3: The index is not a legal requirement. No provision mentions a number. What is required is a suitable and sufficient assessment and, from five employees, a written record of its significant findings (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6)) — and that is the record Orgpuls produces.
body.p4: This is what Orgpuls does not cover: the written health and safety policy (from five employees), the record of your arrangements, procedures to prevent and resolve unacceptable behaviour, the physical work environment, and competent assistance (MHSWR 1999 reg 7). Nor the consultation itself, which Orgpuls records but does not do. The Act and the Regulations apply in Great Britain; in Northern Ireland the same duties to assess and record are in art. 4 of the 1978 Order and MHSWR (NI) 2000, enforced by HSENI.

kontrolltiltak.title: The measurement, consultation and data protection
kontrolltiltak.lead: Consulting representatives or employees, telling employees, reviewing the arrangement, and what data protection law adds.

body.p1: The answers and invitations are personal data under the UK GDPR, even though no single answer can be traced to a person: the Information Commission (ICO) says applying anonymisation itself counts as processing personal data. The ICO also says employees may count as vulnerable data subjects, and recommends a data protection impact assessment if in any doubt.
body.p2: You should be able to show three things: that employees or their representatives were consulted in good time, which the duty to consult supports (SRSC 1977 reg 4A, HSCER 1996 reg 3); that employees know what the survey is for and are told what it found and what is being done (MHSWR 1999 reg 10); and that the arrangement is reviewed.
body.p3: Measurement setup stores this as part of the round rather than as a tick. The consultation is recorded with a date and who it was held with, and the health and safety representative’s involvement is recorded separately.
body.p4: The evaluation has its own cadence on the measurement, and the risk assessment must be reviewed if it may no longer be valid or there has been a significant change (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(3)). It is the part most often forgotten, because it falls due long after everybody has moved on.

rapportTilTilsynet.title: The written record of your risk assessment
rapportTilTilsynet.lead: What it contains, which period it covers, and what to keep with it.

body.p1: The document is built to be your record of the significant findings of the risk assessment and of any group especially at risk (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6)), not a presentation. It is not filed anywhere: you keep it, and an inspector from HSE or the local authority (HSENI in Northern Ireland) may ask to see it (HSWA 1974 s.20(2)(k)). It follows the steps in order: what was surveyed, what the risk assessment concluded, which measures were taken, and what the follow-up showed.
body.p4: Keep with it what Orgpuls does not have: notes of the consultation with representatives or employees, your health and safety policy and the record of your arrangements, and documentation of information and training.

body.p3: The health and safety representative sees the same figures and the same risk assessment as management, and is notified first when a round starts. They do not see individual comments — the law gives representatives no right to information relating specifically to an individual unless that person consents (SRSC 1977 reg 7(2)(c), HSCER 1996 reg 5(3)(c)).
body.p4: Union representative is a position in the register, not a login. It is recorded so that the consultation can be documented, and it grants no access in itself. The same holds for the role field in the register generally: it says who somebody is under the law, not what they may read.

home.sci: The index is a weighted average of the eleven factors, converted from 1–5 to 0–100. A change of less than three points is within normal variation and should not be read as a trend. Source: QPS Nordic user guide (STAMI).

tasks.sci: The research behind QPS Nordic points out that actions aimed at how work is organised work better than individual measures such as stress-management courses. HSE’s guidance on stress likewise says to focus first on organisational issues that affect a group.

measure.s1: The baseline is the full survey. It is taken once a year and sets the zero point.

law.home: The loop on this page is the risk assessment put into a system: assess the risks (MHSWR 1999 reg 3), act on them, and plan, monitor and review the measures (reg 5). The index is not a legal requirement — a suitable and sufficient assessment is, and from five employees a record of its significant findings. The annual cycle covers consultation with employees or their representatives (HSWA 1974 s.2(6), HSCER 1996 reg 3).
law.measure: The law requires no particular method and no particular frequency. It requires a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, reviewed when it may no longer be valid or there has been a significant change (MHSWR 1999 reg 3). HSE lists surveys as one technique for assessing the current situation. The factors here are mapped onto HSE’s Management Standards areas, and the wording is locked so that results stay comparable over time.
law.result: The risk assessment is the requirement itself: MHSWR 1999 reg 3 requires a suitable and sufficient assessment and, from five employees, a record of its significant findings and of any group especially at risk (reg 3(6)). A number alone is not a risk assessment. Hence both factor rows and an overall index, and an assessment per factor.
law.conv: A comment can be about bullying or harassment. It should then be handled under your procedures for unacceptable behaviour, not as an ordinary measure; HSE’s Management Standards look for agreed procedures to prevent or resolve it. The employer must take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of employees (Equality Act 2010 s.40A, Great Britain). A disclosure that someone’s health or safety is endangered can be a qualifying disclosure (ERA 1996 s.43B).
law.tasks: The risk assessment has to be acted on, not just recorded: HSE expects action on the problems it identifies, and MHSWR 1999 reg 5 asks for arrangements to plan, control, monitor and review the measures. That is why an action cannot be closed until its effect has been measured. Representatives are consulted in good time on measures that may substantially affect health and safety (SRSC 1977 reg 4A, HSCER 1996 reg 3).
law.plan: The answers are personal data under the UK GDPR, even though no single answer can be traced to a person, and the legal basis is legal obligation, not consent. Results are shown only for groups that reach the threshold. Employees or their representatives should be consulted in good time, which the duty to consult supports (SRSC 1977 reg 4A, HSCER 1996 reg 3), and employees are told what the assessment found (MHSWR 1999 reg 10).
law.wheel: MHSWR 1999 reg 3(3) requires the risk assessment to be reviewed when there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid or there has been a significant change, whenever in the year that happens. Reg 5 asks for arrangements to monitor and review the measures. The notification order in the annual cycle lets representatives be consulted first.
law.settings: The threshold is not a requirement of health and safety law but follows from data protection law: with few answers, results in small groups can be traced back to individuals, and the Information Commission (ICO) says a person can be identifiable even if you do not know their name. The legal basis is legal obligation under UK GDPR Article 6(1)(c), not consent — the ICO says consent is not usually appropriate in the employment context. The questions are designed not to collect health data (UK GDPR Article 9).
law.report: The written record lies in MHSWR 1999: from five employees, the significant findings of the risk assessment and any group especially at risk (reg 3(6)), and the arrangements for the measures (reg 5(2)); the written health and safety policy is HSWA 1974 s.2(3). Nothing is filed: an inspector from HSE or the local authority may require the documents to be produced (HSWA 1974 s.20(2)(k)). A safety committee, where there is one, keeps the measures under review (s.2(7)).

Results
The answers become an index from 0 to 100 per factor, with a risk band: 65 or above is low risk, 50–64 medium and below 50 high. The result can be read in several ways:

sikkerhet.title: Security, privacy and anonymity | Empvibe
sikkerhet.description: How Empvibe keeps answers anonymous: no link to a person, at least 5 answers per group, data in the EU. What we store, and what we do not.

faq.q: Can the employer see who answered what?
faq.a: No. The answer is stored in a table with no column that could link it to a person. No screen, export or query shows what a named person answered, not even for administrators.

faq.q: What happens when a group is too small?
faq.a: No group is shown before at least 5 have answered; a dash is shown instead. An organisation can raise the threshold to 10, but never lower it below 5. If a hidden group could be calculated from the others, one more group is hidden.

faq.q: Where is the data stored?
faq.a: On servers in the EU (Frankfurt). UK law treats the EEA as adequate for transfers (DPA 2018 Sch 21 paras 4–5). The sub-processors are Supabase, Vercel and Brevo, and Microsoft for organisations that send the survey in Teams.

faq.q: Why is consent not used?
faq.a: Because, as the Information Commission (ICO) puts it, consent is not usually appropriate in the employment context: an employee cannot freely say no to their employer. The basis we recommend is legal obligation, UK GDPR Article 6(1)(c), with the risk assessment under MHSWR 1999 reg 3 (MHSWR (NI) 2000 in Northern Ireland).

faq.q: Are the answers used to train AI?
faq.a: No. We do not share answers with third parties and use no answers to train AI models.

blocks.text: What we store, and what we do not

The register holds each employee’s name, e-mail and group. If you bring in employees from Microsoft Entra ID, the person’s object ID in the directory is stored too. The answer itself goes into a table that **has no column that could hold a link to a person**. The row shows the round, the group and the hour the answer came in – not the minute.

Empvibe recognises the invitation link by a cryptographic checksum. The invitation records that it has been used, so you get no reminder – but never the answer. No screen, export or query shows what a named person answered, not even to administrators: the information does not exist.

items.title: Recognised by a checksum
items.text: The link is looked up by a cryptographic checksum. The invitation only records that it has been used, so you get no reminder.

items.title: Stored with no link to you
items.text: The row shows the round, the group and the hour the answer came in. No column can hold a link to a person.

items.title: Shown only when enough have answered
items.text: Figures are shown per group, and only when the group has at least as many answers as the limit.

blocks.text: Fewer than 5 answers show a dash – always

No group is shown until at least 5 have answered. The database enforces the limit: you can raise it up to 10, but nobody can lower it below 5. The fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what – as the Information Commission (ICO) puts it, a person can be identifiable even if you do not know their name. A round keeps the limit it started with, so lowering the limit later never opens earlier rounds. If the figures for the other groups would reveal a hidden group, Empvibe hides one more, so nobody can work their way back to it.

items.text: No group is shown with fewer. Nobody can lower the limit below 5.

blocks.text: Comments and conversations stay anonymous

A comment is shown only when the group it comes from has enough answers, and the group never travels with the comment. The writer gets a private key to the conversation; the database stores only a checksum of it. If a manager wants to talk directly, the manager can ask – but only the employee can make themselves known, by writing from their own e-mail.
The basis is a legal duty, not consent

The answers are personal data under UK GDPR, even though none can be traced to a person. The basis we recommend is legal obligation: UK GDPR Article 6(1)(c), with the risk assessment under MHSWR 1999 reg 3 (MHSWR (NI) 2000 in Northern Ireland). The Information Commission (ICO) says consent is not usually appropriate in the employment context, so consent is not used. The questions are designed not to collect health data, and answers about violence, threats and offensive behaviour are shown only as counts.
Stored in the EU, not passed on

items: We store the data on servers in the EU (Frankfurt), and UK law treats the EEA as adequate for transfers (DPA 2018 Sch 21 paras 4–5)
We do not share answers with third parties, and use no answers to train AI models

blocks.text: A data processing agreement

You are the controller and Empvibe’s provider, Pundit Invest AS, the processor, under UK GDPR Article 28. The UK version of the agreement is published before Empvibe opens in the United Kingdom; the managing director then reads and signs it under Settings, and can print it or save it as PDF. We use three sub-processors: Supabase (database and sign-in, Frankfurt), Vercel (hosting, Frankfurt) and Brevo (e-mail), and a fourth for organisations that send the survey in Teams: Microsoft (Azure Bot Service, EU).
Questions to ask any supplier
Anonymity is easy to promise and hard to prove. Ask these questions – of us and of others:

items: Is there any column or log that could link an answer to a person – including for administrators?
How large must a group be before it is shown, and who can lower the threshold?
Can a hidden group be calculated from the total and the other groups?
Does the group come with a comment when it is shown?
Where is the data stored, and which sub-processors are used?
Are the answers used for anything else, such as training AI models?

smaaBedrifter.kicker: For small businesses with no HR team
smaaBedrifter.h1: Staff wellbeing survey for small businesses – set up in under an hour
smaaBedrifter.lead: Small businesses rarely have an HR department, but the duty to assess the risk of work-related stress applies from the first employee. Empvibe is a staff survey that handles sending, reminders and the written record. You spend your time on what comes out of it.

blocks.text: What about anonymity when we are few?

It is the first question in a small business, and the right one to ask. Empvibe shows results only for groups of at least 5 respondents. If you are 12, you see figures for the whole business, but not for a team of 3: their answers count in the whole, never on their own.

In the UK the limit is 5 and cannot be lowered; you can raise it to 10. It lives in the database, and a survey keeps the limit it opened with. The answer is stored without name, e-mail address or IP address, and no column can link an answer to a person.

blocks.title: Fewer than five of you?
blocks.text: Then the whole business is one group that never reaches 5 answers, so Empvibe shows no figures and no comments at all – not for you, not for anyone. With 5 to 9 answers you see the whole business only: any split into teams leaves a group under 5. You still assess the risk, and in a small business, HSE notes, consulting people individually is often effective.
What the law asks – by headcount

Every employer must assess the risks to its employees' health and safety, stress included, from the first employee. What changes at five is how much you write down. These are the rules in Great Britain; in Northern Ireland the assessment and its records are in MHSWR (NI) 2000, enforced by HSENI.

items.title: Assess the risks, stress included, and act on them
items.text: A suitable and sufficient risk assessment, reviewed when it may no longer be valid. MHSWR 1999 reg 3.

items.title: Consult your employees
items.text: In good time, directly or through a union-appointed or elected representative. No headcount rule. SRSC 1977, HSCER 1996.

items.title: Write down the significant findings
items.text: And any group of employees identified as especially at risk. MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6).

items.title: Record your arrangements
items.text: How you plan, organise, control, monitor and review the measures. MHSWR 1999 reg 5(2).

items.title: A written health and safety policy
items.text: Brought to every employee's notice; the count is per undertaking. HSWA 1974 s.2(3), SI 1975/1584.

blocks.text: Read more about [what the law asks about work-related stress](/lovkrav).
Simpler – but not optional

The rules take your size into account: your arrangements must be appropriate to the nature of your activities and the size of your undertaking (MHSWR 1999 reg 5(1)), and with fewer than five employees the assessment need not be written down – though HSE notes it is useful, so you can review it later. But the duty to assess the risk and act on it applies all the same.

blocks.title: In a small business, everything shows
blocks.text: When one person is off sick or leaves, everyone notices. That is why a simple, fixed rhythm pays off more for a small business than for a large one – not less.
Where a survey fits

No UK law requires a survey, or names the factors to ask about: the law asks for the risk assessment. HSE lists surveys among the ways to assess the current situation, alongside existing data and other techniques. So a survey can form part of your stress risk assessment – the findings are what you write down and act on.

Empvibe asks about eleven factors of the psychosocial work environment, in wording that builds on QPS Nordic, a validated Nordic research questionnaire, and maps them onto the areas of HSE's Management Standards. The mapping is our own, Change is touched by one statement only, and the Standards are guidance, not law.
The time it takes

head: What
Time
rows: Signing up with your company number

blocks.text: Setting up without an HR team

Paste employees in from a spreadsheet or add them one at a time – you do not need an HR system. If you use Microsoft Entra ID, they can come from there. Send the survey by e-mail, in Microsoft Teams or Slack, or share it as a link or a QR code in the break room for people who do not sit at a PC. An e-mail address is optional, but without one the system cannot send that person a reminder.
A year in a small business

items.title: Sign up
items.text: With your Companies House number (limited companies and LLPs). Add employees from a spreadsheet.

items.title: Send the survey
items.text: About 4 minutes per employee, with one reminder from the system.

items.title: Go through the results
items.text: With your employees, or their health and safety representative if you have one. From five employees, write the significant findings down.

items.title: Choose two or three measures
items.text: Each with an owner and a deadline.

items.title: Measure again
items.text: A short pulse on the factors where measures are running, and the next annual survey in a year.

blocks.text: What you get

items: An annual survey of 11 factors, with short pulses in between
The findings that matter most, turned into measures with an owner and a deadline
Your written record of the significant findings and any group especially at risk (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6))
Anonymous comments you can reply to without learning who wrote them
The same figures for your health and safety representative, if you have one

blocks.title: What stays yours
blocks.text: Empvibe gives you the survey, the action plan and a written record of the findings. From five employees you also need a written health and safety policy and a record of your arrangements – those are yours to write. So is the consultation: Empvibe records it, but the conversation is yours.

faq.q: Does a small business have to assess the risk of stress?
faq.a: Yes. Every employer must make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks to its employees' health and safety (MHSWR 1999 reg 3; in Northern Ireland, MHSWR (NI) 2000 reg 3), and HSE applies that duty to work-related stress. With fewer than five employees you don't have to write it down, though HSE notes it is useful to; from five, you record the significant findings (reg 3(6)).

faq.q: Do we have to run a survey?
faq.a: No. No UK law requires a survey or names the factors to ask about – the law asks for the risk assessment. HSE lists surveys as one way to assess the current situation, so a survey can form part of your stress risk assessment. What counts is that you act on what it finds.

faq.q: What if only four answer?
faq.a: Then no figures are shown: a dash appears instead of a number. The figure is not hidden from you in particular – it is not calculated for anyone. In the UK the limit is 5 and cannot be lowered, so a business where fewer than five people answer gets no results from the survey. That is what it takes for nobody to recognise an answer.

faq.q: Do we need an HR system?
faq.a: No. Paste employees in from a spreadsheet or add them one at a time. An e-mail address is optional if you share the survey as a link or a QR code, but without one the system cannot send that person a reminder.

faq.q: Do we need a health and safety representative?
faq.a: Not necessarily, and there is no headcount rule. If a recognised trade union has appointed safety representatives, you consult them (SRSC 1977). If not, you consult employees directly or through representatives they elect (HSCER 1996 reg 4; in Northern Ireland, HSCER (NI) 1996). You do not choose the representative. If you have one, they see the same figures in Empvibe.

faq.q: Do we send the record to HSE?
faq.a: No. Nothing is filed anywhere. You keep the record, and an inspector (HSE or your local authority; HSENI in Northern Ireland) may ask to see it (in Great Britain, HSWA 1974 s.20(2)(k)).

faq.q: Does this apply in Northern Ireland?
faq.a: Yes, under its own regulations: MHSWR (NI) 2000 for the risk assessment and its records, and HSCER (NI) 1996 for consulting employees. The regulator is HSENI. The other references on this page are to the law in Great Britain.

lovkrav.title: Stress risk assessment: what the law requires | Empvibe
lovkrav.description: What the law requires of UK employers on work-related stress: the risk assessment, the record from five employees, consultation and HSE's Management Standards.
lovkrav.h1: What does the law require of an employer on work-related stress, and where does a survey fit?
lovkrav.lead: No UK statute names the stress factors an employer must survey, and none requires a survey. What the law does require is that an employer ensures, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of its employees (HSWA 1974 s.2), and makes a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks to their health and safety (MHSWR 1999 reg 3). The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) says that duty covers stress. With five or more employees, the significant findings must be recorded. Employees or their representatives are consulted, whatever your size. Northern Ireland has the same duties in its own legislation.

blocks.text: What the law requires – and what it does not

In Great Britain the starting point is the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. [Section 2(1)](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1974/37/section/2) makes it the duty of every employer to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all its employees. The Act's definition of personal injury includes any impairment of a person's mental condition (s.53(1)), so the duty covers mental as well as physical health. The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 add the method: assess the risks ([reg 3](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3242/regulation/3)), and make arrangements to plan, organise, control, monitor and review the measures (reg 5). Northern Ireland has its own twins, set out below.
Employers have a legal duty to protect workers from stress at work by doing a risk assessment and acting on it. This is the same duty you have to protect people from other health and safety risks.
blocks.cite: HSE, [Work-related stress and how to manage it](https://www.hse.gov.uk/stress/overview.htm)

blocks.text: What the law does not do is name the factors to look at or prescribe a method. There is no statutory questionnaire and no duty to run a staff survey. HSE's Management Standards describe six areas of work design to look at, but they are guidance, not law. HSE says they allow assessment of the current situation using “pre-existing data, surveys and other techniques”: a survey is one way to gather what the assessment needs, not a requirement in itself.

items.text: Ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all employees.
Make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks to employees' health and safety, and review it when it may no longer be valid or things have changed significantly.
With five or more employees, record the significant findings and any group identified as especially at risk.
Arrangements to plan, organise, control, monitor and review the measures, recorded with five or more employees.
Give employees comprehensible and relevant information on the risks identified and the measures taken.
Consult union-appointed safety representatives; where employees have none, consult them directly or through representatives they elect.
The 1978 Order (art. 4) and MHSWR (NI) 2000: the same general duty, the same risk assessment and the same records from five employees.

blocks.text: The risk assessment, step by step

HSE sums up the minimum the 1999 Regulations require in three steps: identify what could cause injury or illness in your business (the hazards); decide how likely it is that someone could be harmed and how seriously (the risk); and take action to eliminate the hazard or, if that isn't possible, control the risk. For stress, HSE says you should assess the risk “in the same way as you assess other work-related health and safety risks” ([Stress risk assessment](https://www.hse.gov.uk/stress/risk-assessment.htm)). The regulations add a record and a review.

items.title: Identify the hazards
items.text: What in the work could cause harm. For stress, HSE's Management Standards point to six areas of work design.

items.title: Decide the risk
items.text: Who could be harmed, how likely it is and how seriously. HSE advises looking first at issues that affect groups of employees.

items.title: Take action
items.text: Plan, organise, control, monitor and review the measures. HSE advises removing the cause where you can, and otherwise controlling the risk.

items.title: Record and review
items.text: From five employees, record the significant findings. Review when the assessment may no longer be valid or things have changed significantly.

blocks.text: Employees must be given comprehensible and relevant information on the risks the assessment identifies and the measures taken (MHSWR 1999 reg 10). The review is tied to circumstances, not to a calendar: reason to suspect the assessment is no longer valid, or a significant change in the matters it relates to (reg 3(3)).
Stress and HSE's Management Standards

The [Management Standards](https://www.hse.gov.uk/stress/standards/) are HSE's approach to the stress part of the assessment. HSE says they cover “six key areas of work design that, if not properly managed, are associated with poor health, lower productivity and increased accident and sickness absence rates”. For each area HSE describes a standard, and states to be achieved that organisations should work towards.

head: Area
What it covers (HSE)
The standard (HSE)
rows: “This includes issues such as workload, work patterns, and the work environment.”
“employees indicate that they are able to cope with the demands of their jobs”
“How much say the person has in the way they do their work.”
“employees indicate that they are able to have a say about the way they do their work”
“This includes the encouragement, sponsorship and resources provided by the organisation, line management and colleagues.”
“employees indicate that they receive adequate information and support from their colleagues and superiors”
“This includes promoting positive working to avoid conflict and dealing with unacceptable behaviour.”
“employees indicate that they are not subjected to unacceptable behaviours, eg bullying at work”
“This includes whether people understand their role within the organisation and whether the organisation ensures that the person does not have conflicting roles.”
“employees indicate that they understand their role and responsibilities”
“This includes how organisational change (large or small) is managed and communicated in the organisation.”
“employees indicate that the organisation engages them frequently when undergoing an organisational change”

blocks.text: Every standard has a second part as well: “systems are in place locally to respond to any individual concerns.”
The Management Standards are not new laws.

HSE does not expect an employer to meet all the standards. They are “a target for the organisation, goals that employers should be working towards through an ongoing process of risk assessment and continuous improvement”. Nor are they the only route. HSE says that if you follow the approach correctly, you will be adopting “an approach that is considered suitable and sufficient”; HSENI, Northern Ireland's regulator, says an alternative approach is possible, but it “must include a suitable and sufficient risk assessment”.
HSE sets the approach out in [five steps](https://www.hse.gov.uk/stress/standards/), after preparing the organisation:

items: Identify the risk factors
Who can be harmed and how
Evaluate the risks
Record your findings
Monitor and review

blocks.text: What to write down from five employees

With five or more employees, the regulations ask for two records: the **significant findings** of the risk assessment, with any group of employees it identifies as **especially at risk** (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6)); and your **arrangements** for planning, organising, controlling, monitoring and reviewing the measures (reg 5(2)). In Great Britain a written health and safety policy is also required from five employees (HSWA 1974 s.2(3); SI 1975/1584). With fewer than five, the assessment is still required but need not be written down – though HSE notes that a record is useful, so you can review it later.

The records are yours. Nothing is filed with HSE or anyone else: you keep them, and an inspector may ask to see them (HSWA 1974 s.20(2)(k)). The regulations do not set a format. A department whose results stand out may be a group especially at risk; that is your judgement to make and write down. To make the record easy to follow up, it helps if it also shows:

items: what you looked at, when and how – a survey, absence figures, conversations
the significant findings, and any group especially at risk
who was consulted, and how
the measures chosen, with an owner and a deadline for each
whether the measures worked, and when you will look again

blocks.title: A survey is one source, not the whole assessment
blocks.text: A questionnaire shows how employees see their work. Sickness absence figures, conversations in teams and what representatives raise can show what a questionnaire misses. What matters is that the record shows what you found, how you judged it and what you did about it.
Who must be consulted

Every employer must consult employees on health and safety, and there is no headcount threshold. Which regulations apply depends on whether a recognised trade union has appointed safety representatives: if it has, the Safety Representatives and Safety Committees Regulations 1977 (SRSC); for employees they do not represent, the Health and Safety (Consultation with Employees) Regulations 1996 (HSCER). There, HSE says you can choose to consult “directly as individuals, or through elected health and safety representatives (known as ‘representatives of employee safety’ in the Regulations), or a combination of the two” ([What the law says about consulting workers](https://www.hse.gov.uk/involvement/prepare/law/index.htm)).

center.title: The employer
center.text: Carries the duty to assess the risk and act on it (HSWA 1974 s.2, MHSWR 1999 reg 3), and the duty to consult.

items.title: Union safety representatives
items.text: Appointed by a recognised trade union (SRSC 1977 reg 3). Consult them in good time, including on any measure that may substantially affect the health and safety of those they represent (reg 4A). If two or more ask in writing, a safety committee must be set up within three months (reg 9).

items.title: Elected representatives
items.text: Where employees have no union safety representative, you may consult representatives of employee safety whom the employees have elected (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(b)). You cannot choose them yourself.

items.title: Employees directly
items.text: With no representative, you consult the employees themselves (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(a)). HSE notes that in a small business this is often effective.

blocks.title: Talk to people before the survey
blocks.text: Whether starting a survey is itself a measure you must consult on is a question of interpretation. Consulting anyway is good practice: tell employees, and any representatives, what will be asked, who will see which results and what happens next.
What an inspector may ask for
In Great Britain, health and safety law is enforced by inspectors from HSE or your local authority; in Northern Ireland, by HSENI. Three provisions of the 1974 Act matter here:

items.title: Documents
items.text: An inspector may require you to produce, and may inspect and copy, the documents the law requires you to keep – such as the record of your risk assessment (HSWA 1974 s.20(2)(k)).

items.title: Improvement notice
items.text: Where an inspector is of the opinion that you are breaching a legal requirement, or have done so in a way likely to continue or be repeated, they may serve an improvement notice (s.21).

items.title: Directors and managers
items.text: Where a company's offence is committed with the consent or connivance of a director or manager, or is attributable to their neglect, that person can be guilty of it as well (s.37(1)).

blocks.text: HSE says it will only consider investigating work-related stress “where it is evident that several employees are experiencing work-related stress or related ill health”, and will not generally investigate individual cases. Nor will it investigate where concerns have not already been raised with the employer and the employer has not had enough time to respond. Bullying and harassment, HSE says, should be referred to Acas ([Reporting a concern](https://www.hse.gov.uk/stress/reporting-concern.htm)).
HSE expects organisations to carry out a suitable and sufficient risk assessment for stress, and to take action to tackle any problems identified by that risk assessment.
Northern Ireland: the same duties, its own law

The 1974 Act does not extend to Northern Ireland (HSWA 1974 s.84(1)), and nor do the 1999 Regulations. Northern Ireland has its own twins. Article 4 of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978 sets the same general duty. The [Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2000](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisr/2000/388/regulation/3) require the same risk assessment and, with five or more employees, the same records (regs 3(6) and 5(2)). Where employees have no union safety representatives, the Health and Safety (Consultation with Employees) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1996 give the same choice: consult them directly or through elected representatives. The regulator is HSENI.

There is no legislation that specifically mentions work-related stress however under Article 4 of the Health and Safety at Work Order (NI) 1978 employers have a duty to ensure so far as is reasonably practicable the health, safety and welfare of employees at work.

HSENI says it will undertake enforcement action where the legally required suitable and sufficient risk assessment has not been carried out, and that an organisation “would be unlikely to be subject to enforcement action by HSENI provided it could demonstrate it had adequately assessed the risks and was taking steps to address any problems identified”.
Where a survey fits

A survey can form part of your stress risk assessment. Each Management Standard is written as what employees indicate, so asking employees, anonymously, is a direct way to see where you stand. Results by department show where to look first, in line with HSE's advice to focus first on organisational issues that affect groups. A survey does not make the decisions for you: you still judge what is significant, decide what to do and write it down.

blocks.title: How Empvibe fits
blocks.text: Empvibe surveys eleven factors of the psychosocial work environment, in wording that builds on QPS Nordic, a validated Nordic research questionnaire. We map the factors onto HSE's six Management Standards areas; the mapping is our own, and Change is touched by one statement only. [Results](/plattform#resultater) are shown by factor and department, only for groups of at least five. [Measures](/plattform#tiltak) get an owner and a deadline, a pulse survey shows whether they worked, and you get a [written record](/plattform#rapport) for your risk assessment. An organisation can also add HSE's Management Standards Indicator Tool, unchanged, as a module. Contains public sector information published by the Health and Safety Executive and licensed under the Open Government Licence.

See [how the platform works](/plattform), [how anonymity is protected](/sikkerhet), and what it means for [health and safety representatives](/verneombud) and for [small businesses](/smaa-bedrifter). HSE's own guidance is at [Stress and mental health at work](https://www.hse.gov.uk/stress/).

faq.q: Is a stress survey a legal requirement?
faq.a: No. No UK law requires a staff survey. The law requires a suitable and sufficient risk assessment that covers work-related stress, and action on what it finds (MHSWR 1999 reg 3; in Northern Ireland, MHSWR (NI) 2000 reg 3). HSE lists surveys as one technique for the assessment, alongside existing data and other methods. A survey can form part of your stress risk assessment, but it is not the assessment on its own.

faq.q: Do I need to write the risk assessment down?
faq.a: With five or more employees, yes. You must record the significant findings and any group of employees identified as especially at risk (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6); the same in Northern Ireland), and your arrangements for planning, organising, controlling, monitoring and reviewing the measures (reg 5(2)). With fewer than five, the assessment is still required but need not be written down. HSE notes that a record is still useful, so you can review it later.

faq.q: Are the Management Standards the law?
faq.a: No. In HSE's words, “The Management Standards are not new laws.” They are HSE's guidance for the stress part of the risk assessment, covering six areas: demands, control, support, relationships, role and change. HSE does not expect an employer to meet all the standards. Following the approach correctly is, HSE says, an approach considered suitable and sufficient, but the legal duty is the risk assessment itself.

faq.q: What if we have no safety representative?
faq.a: That is lawful: there is no duty to have one. A recognised trade union may appoint safety representatives, and employees may elect representatives for you to consult, but you cannot choose a representative yourself. Where there is none, you consult employees directly (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(a); Northern Ireland's 1996 regulations give the same choice). The duty to consult applies whatever your size.

faq.q: How often should we review the risk assessment?
faq.a: The regulations tie the review to circumstances, not to a fixed interval. In Great Britain you must review the assessment if there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid, or if there has been a significant change in the matters it relates to, and make any changes needed (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(3)). A regular survey, and a short pulse after a change, can show when that point has come.

faq.q: Who enforces the law on work-related stress?
faq.a: In Great Britain, inspectors from HSE or the local authority; in Northern Ireland, HSENI. An inspector may require you to produce the documents the law requires you to keep, such as the record of your risk assessment (HSWA 1974 s.20(2)(k)), and may serve an improvement notice (s.21). HSE says it will only consider investigating work-related stress where it is evident that several employees are experiencing work-related stress or related ill health.

faq.q: Does the same law apply in Northern Ireland?
faq.a: The same duties apply, under Northern Ireland's own legislation. The HSWA 1974 and the MHSWR 1999 extend to Great Britain only. In Northern Ireland the general duty is in article 4 of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978, and the risk assessment and the records from five employees are in the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2000. The regulator is HSENI.

faq.q: Is the duty the company's or the managing director's?
faq.a: The duty is the employer's, which for a company is the company itself (HSWA 1974 s.2(1); in Northern Ireland, art. 4(1) of the 1978 Order). But in Great Britain, where a company commits an offence with the consent or connivance of a director or manager, or through their neglect, that person can be guilty of it too (HSWA 1974 s.37(1)). A union safety representative's functions impose no duty on them (SRSC 1977 reg 4(1)); the assessment stays with the employer.

verneombud.title: Safety representatives and stress risk assessment | Empvibe
verneombud.description: Health and safety representatives and employee consultation in a stress risk assessment: who they are, their part at each step, and what to do without one.
verneombud.h1: Health and safety representatives and the stress survey: consultation step by step
verneombud.lead: Every employer must consult employees on health and safety, and work-related stress is part of it. Where a recognised trade union has appointed safety representatives, the employer consults them in good time; otherwise it consults employees directly or through representatives they have elected. Here is what representatives can expect at each step of a stress survey — and what to do if you have none. The responsibility stays with the employer.

blocks.text: Who represents employees

Health and safety law in Great Britain recognises two kinds of representative. Where an employer recognises a trade union, the union may appoint **safety representatives** from among the employees (SRSC 1977 reg 3). Other employees are consulted directly or through **representatives of employee safety** they have elected (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)). HSE calls both kinds health and safety representatives. Neither depends on headcount, an organisation may lawfully have neither, and HSE is clear: “As an employer, you cannot decide who the representative will be.”

center.title: The employer
center.text: Consults in good time on health and safety, and keeps the responsibility for the risk assessment and the measures (SRSC 1977 reg 4A; HSCER 1996 reg 3).

items.title: Union safety representative
items.text: Appointed from among the employees by a recognised trade union, whatever the headcount (SRSC 1977 reg 3).

items.title: Representative of employee safety
items.text: Elected by a group of employees not represented by a union, to be consulted on their behalf (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(b)).

items.title: The employees directly
items.text: Where no representative speaks for them, the employer consults employees as individuals (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(a)).

items.title: Safety committee (if you have one)
items.text: Must be set up within three months when two union safety representatives ask for one in writing (SRSC 1977 reg 9).

blocks.text: The employer’s duty to consult

The duty to consult applies to every employer. Union safety representatives are consulted so that employer and employees can co-operate on health and safety measures “and in checking the effectiveness of such measures” (HSWA 1974 s.2(6); in Northern Ireland, art. 4(5) of the 1978 Order). Consultation must come **in good time**, in particular on any measure that may substantially affect health and safety (SRSC 1977 reg 4A; HSCER 1996 reg 3). Stress is no exception: HSE calls the duty to assess it “the same duty you have to protect people from other health and safety risks”. Whether starting a survey is itself such a measure is a matter of interpretation; consulting before it goes out is good practice that the duty supports.

items.text: A recognised trade union may appoint safety representatives from among the employees, with no minimum headcount. They have their functions once the employer has their names in writing.
They may investigate hazards and complaints, make representations to the employer and represent employees with inspectors — rights, not duties. The employer must consult them in good time.
They may inspect and copy documents the employer must keep and get the information their functions need — but not information relating specifically to an individual, unless that person consents.
If at least two safety representatives ask in writing, the employer must set up a safety committee within three months.
Employees without union safety representatives are consulted in good time, directly or through representatives of employee safety they have elected, whose names and groups the employer makes known.

HSENI enforces. Union safety representatives come under the 1979 Northern Ireland regulations; the Health and Safety (Consultation with Employees) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1996 give the same choice of direct or elected consultation.

blocks.text: Your role at each step

items.title: Be consulted before the survey goes out — not told afterwards.
items.text: **Ask:** When will it run, who will receive it, and when will we hear the results?

items.title: Know what is asked, and be able to explain why it is safe to answer.
items.text: **Ask:** Which areas of work do the questions cover, and how is anonymity secured?

items.title: See the same figures as management — not a summary afterwards.
items.text: **Ask:** Do I see what management sees, and are groups under 5 hidden for everyone?

items.title: Take part when measures are chosen, and check that they tackle the causes.
items.text: **Ask:** Does every measure have an owner and a deadline, and how will we check that it worked?

items.title: See that the significant findings are written down and kept.
items.text: **Ask:** Where is our record of the findings and of any group especially at risk, and who keeps it?

blocks.text: What representatives should be able to see

items.title: The same figures as management
items.text: Results by factor and department, for groups of at least 5 — the basis the risk is assessed on, not a summary afterwards.

items.title: The measures
items.text: Which measures were chosen, who owns each one, its deadline, and how it will be checked that it worked.

items.title: How anonymity works
items.text: What is stored and how small a group can be shown, so you can tell colleagues why it is safe to answer.

items.title: The written record
items.text: With five or more employees, the significant findings and any group especially at risk are recorded (MHSWR 1999 reg 3(6); in Northern Ireland, MHSWR (NI) 2000 reg 3(6)). Union safety representatives may inspect and copy it (SRSC 1977 reg 7).

blocks.title: What Empvibe does — and what it does not
blocks.text: Empvibe runs the survey, shows results by factor and department for groups of at least 5, keeps each measure with an owner and a deadline, checks it with a pulse, and produces a written record for your risk assessment. A health and safety representative, where you have one, gets a role that sees the same figures as management. Empvibe does not consult for you: talking with representatives or employees about the plan, the findings and the measures is the employer’s job. And a survey is one source for the risk assessment, not all of it.
If you have no representative

Then you consult employees directly, which the law allows (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(a)). HSE: “If you have a small business, or you have regular contact with all your employees, consulting with individuals is often effective.” Give employees the information they need to take part fully and effectively (reg 5(1)): in practice, the plan before the survey, the results after it, and a say before measures are chosen. If you switch from elected representatives to consulting employees directly, tell both (reg 4(4)).
When you want to raise it with management

Do you think the risk of work-related stress has not been assessed, but are unsure how to raise it? Start with questions, not demands: when did we last assess it, what did we find, and what happened to the findings? HSE expects organisations “to carry out a suitable and sufficient risk assessment for stress, and to take action to tackle any problems identified by that risk assessment”. A survey can form part of that assessment. Read more about [what the law requires](/lovkrav).

blocks.title: Advice from practice
blocks.text: Raise it as a question of rhythm, not of a tool: “When did we last look at stress, and what happened to the findings?” The answer usually says more than any survey.
When management does not act

The law gives representatives a route. Union safety representatives can make representations to the employer (SRSC 1977 reg 4(1)(d)), elected representatives can do the same for their group (HSCER 1996 reg 6), and two union safety representatives can ask in writing for a safety committee (SRSC 1977 reg 9). The last step is an inspector (HSE or your local authority; HSENI in Northern Ireland). HSE’s guidance on consultation says inspectors “can enforce for failure to comply with legal duties on procedural matters”.

items.title: Raise it
items.text: With your line manager or the managing director, preferably in writing.

items.title: Point to the figures
items.text: Which factors, which groups, and how they have developed.

items.title: Ask for a safety committee
items.text: If you are union safety representatives: two of you ask in writing, and it must be set up within three months.

items.title: Go to an inspector
items.text: HSE considers investigating stress only where several employees are affected, and once the employer has had the concern and time to respond.

blocks.text: Bullying or harassment of an individual takes a different route. HSE writes that it “is not the appropriate body to investigate bullying or harassment” and refers such issues to Acas; in Northern Ireland, HSENI says the LRA is better placed to advise on individual employee relations cases.
When a department is not shown

In Empvibe, results are shown only for groups of at least 5 respondents. An organisation may raise the limit to 10, but never lower it below 5. When a small department is not shown, nobody is hiding anything from you: the figure has not been calculated for anyone, precisely so that nobody can tell who answered what. The answers still count in the figures for the whole organisation. Read more about [how anonymity works](/sikkerhet).

faq.q: Must we have a health and safety representative?
faq.a: No. There is no headcount rule, and an organisation may lawfully have no representative. A recognised trade union may appoint safety representatives (SRSC 1977 reg 3), and employees may be consulted through representatives of employee safety they have elected (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(b)). Where there are none, the employer consults employees directly (HSCER 1996 reg 4(1)(a)). The duty to consult applies either way.

faq.q: Can the employer choose the representative?
faq.a: No. A trade union appoints safety representatives, and employees elect representatives of employee safety. HSE: “As an employer, you cannot decide who the representative will be.” What the employer may choose, for employees not represented by a union, is whether to consult them directly, through elected representatives, or both.

faq.q: Can management see who answered what?
faq.a: No. No single answer can be traced to a person: the answer table has no column that could link it to anyone, and results are shown only for groups of at least 5 respondents. The representative sees the same figures as management. Nor does the law entitle representatives to information relating specifically to an individual without that person’s consent (SRSC 1977 reg 7(2)(c)).

faq.q: Is a stress survey required by law?
faq.a: No. The law requires a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, work-related stress included (MHSWR 1999 reg 3; in Northern Ireland, MHSWR (NI) 2000 reg 3). A survey can form part of your stress risk assessment: HSE lists surveys among the techniques for assessing the current situation. HSE’s Management Standards are guidance: “The Management Standards are not new laws.”

faq.q: Do we need a safety committee?
faq.a: Only if at least two union safety representatives ask for one in writing. The employer must then set it up within three months (SRSC 1977 reg 9). There is no headcount trigger, and the 1996 regulations for employees without union representation contain no committee route.

faq.q: Should the representative take part in the risk assessment?
faq.a: They should be consulted on it. The employer must consult in good time on the health and safety information employees must be given (SRSC 1977 reg 4A(1)(c); HSCER 1996 reg 3), and that includes the risks the assessment found and the measures (MHSWR 1999 reg 10, Great Britain). Whether starting the survey itself requires prior consultation is a matter of interpretation; consulting before it goes out is good practice that the duty supports.

faq.q: What if management does not act?
faq.a: Raise it in writing, with the figures. Union safety representatives can make representations to the employer and, two together, ask in writing for a safety committee (SRSC 1977 regs 4 and 9); elected representatives can make representations for their group (HSCER 1996 reg 6). The last step is an inspector (HSE or your local authority; HSENI in Northern Ireland). HSE does not investigate stress until the concern has been raised with the employer and it has had time to respond.

body: I would like to suggest that we survey work-related stress{inOrg}. We must make a suitable and sufficient risk assessment that covers stress (MHSWR 1999 reg 3; in Northern Ireland, MHSWR (NI) 2000 reg 3), and a survey can form part of it. As health and safety representative I would like us to get started, and to be consulted from the planning stage.

I have looked at Empvibe, a survey of the psychosocial work environment that maps its factors onto the areas of HSE’s Management Standards for work-related stress. No single answer can be traced to a person, and results are shown only for groups of at least 5. We would get results by factor and department, measures with an owner and a deadline, and a written record for our risk assessment.
The health and safety representative can have a role that sees the same figures as management, so do add me as health and safety representative when it is set up.
You can read more and get started here: {link}
Could we bring it up at the next meeting?
